source.title: How Much of Your Data Can Suck? Thresholds for Domain Performance and Emergent Misalignment in LLMs
source.authors: Jian Ouyang; T. Arman; Ge Jin

record.tranche_reason: Tests safety-related outcomes after supervised fine-tuning with different proportions and types of incorrect domain data, a new data-quality setting rather than the specified harmful- or benign-example fine-tuning recipes.
record.gate_note: The paper reports harmful/misaligned output measures after fine-tuning on incorrect data, so those outcomes are recorded. Its training data are not identified as ordinary benign instruction data or as a small set of harmful-request examples. It reports no token-position KL, compliant-prefix, suffix, decoding, weight-localization, shallowness-mechanism, or safety-deepening results. Table 9 duplicates Table 7 and is not counted again.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes gpt-4o on 6000 domain examples with varying shares of incorrect answers. It measures emergent misalignment, an Evil Rate on the Betley et al. benchmark of unrelated moral prompts, and domain accuracy. It does not measure compliance with harmful requests after a few to a few hundred harmful examples (V1). Its training data are deliberately incorrect, not benign (V2). It has no token-position, prefill or decoding, localization, mechanism or deepening experiments (V3–V7). Emergent misalignment is a related but different construct, so the findings go under fits_no_version. The paper only cites Qi et al. in its introduction. The reader's 'tests/T3' contradicts its own all-'not_tested' version statuses and all-'none' rows.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right but hides an internal inconsistency. The abstract and Section 3.1 say modest incorrect data (10–25%) does not significantly affect moral alignment. The tables show Evil Rate rising only at 75–90% incorrect data. Yet the Analysis, Discussion and Conclusion claim that even 10% incorrect data sharply raises misalignment. The authors also say at least 50% correct data is needed to recover, that fine-tuned models rarely match base gpt-4o, and that practitioners should curate data rigorously or avoid fine-tuning.
record.recipe_differences: The paper varies the proportions of correct and overtly or subtly incorrect domain-specific SFT data, using 6000 examples per training run and one epoch. It does not use the specified small harmful-request or benign-instruction fine-tuning intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by domain, correctness ratio, and obvious versus subtle error type. The authors state that subtle incorrect data notably worsened moral alignment in finance and legal, but not health; code models retained 0% Evil (4–5) completions across listed ratios.

fits_no_version.finding: Finance SFT gives Evil Rates of 22.5% (obvious) and 38.9% (subtle) at 10% correct data, 9.5% and 5.0% at 25%, and 0.0% at 50% or more correct. The base model is 0.0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SFT on mostly incorrect domain data induces emergent misalignment on unrelated moral prompts, with a threshold near 50% correct data.

fits_no_version.finding: Legal SFT gives Evil Rates of 29.7% (obvious) and 46.5% (subtle) at 10% correct, 2.3% for obvious at 25% correct, and 0.0% elsewhere.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SFT on mostly incorrect domain data induces emergent misalignment on unrelated moral prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Code SFT on insecure or incorrect code gives 0% Evil (4–5) completions at every ratio. Health shows no notable subtle-versus-obvious difference, according to the prose.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment from incorrect-data SFT varies by domain.

record.problems: The study uses one model family and LLM-judged evaluations on synthetically generated sets of 100 domain questions. It says each cell was repeated with three seeds but supplies no uncertainty estimates. The text provides no clear health moral-alignment table; the health prose reports only a qualitative comparison. The legal moral-alignment table is flattened, making later model-to-value assignments less secure. The paper's summary statements about the impact of modest incorrect-data amounts are not fully consistent across sections. The base-model summary tables also present different aggregate correct-rate figures.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 and Tables 6, 8, and 10 primarily report domain technical-performance scores, not the harmful-completion outcome catalogued here. Table 9 duplicates Table 7. No further harmful-completion results were left out.

untested.parts: Few-to-few-hundred harmful-example fine-tuning and harmful-request compliance are not tested. Training uses 6000 incorrect-answer examples, and the outcome is emergent misalignment on unrelated prompts.
Benign data is not used; the incorrect domain data is deliberately wrong and partly dangerous.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.

missing.what: Health-domain moral-alignment (Evil Rate) results are discussed in prose and in Figure 2, but no table appears in the text. Table 8 is mislabelled 'Finance' and gives health technical performance only.

record.verdict_notes: This is an emergent-misalignment study, not a shallow-alignment study. It uses one model (gpt-4o via the OpenAI API), LLM judges, 100 synthetic questions per domain, and reports no uncertainty despite three seeds. The claim that no RLHF was applied is odd for gpt-4o-2024-08-06, which is itself safety-trained. The code 'subtle' subset is missing. Table 9 duplicates Table 7.

versions.untested_parts: The study fine-tunes on 6000 domain examples per run with varying fractions of incorrect data; it does not test a few to a few hundred harmful-request examples or measure refusal/compliance on harmful requests as such.
The fine-tuning data are incorrect domain answers, not ordinary or carefully chosen benign instruction data.
No per-token KL or aligned-versus-base output-distribution measurement.
No compliant-prefix, suffix, or decoding-change experiment.
No weight or rank localization experiment.
Does not test why safety behaviour is shallow or whether data or objective causes shallowness.
No training intended to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deepened safety holds up.
